summary: Children build fluent, usable knowledge that landmark fractions (1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/5, 2/5, 4/5 and tenths/hundredths) have partner percentage and decimal forms, and — crucially — deploy those equivalences to solve problems (25% off £40; 20% of 60). The core is procedural: recognise which landmark applies, convert to the handiest form, and compute. Ground every equivalent on a hundred-grid or bar so 'per cent = per hundred' stays concrete, and build a benchmark toolkit (50% = halve, 10% = ÷10, 1% = ÷100, 25% = ÷4) that children combine to reach any whole-number target percentage rather than memorising isolated facts. Always require interpreting the answer in context (discount vs sale price).
misconceptions: Base-neglect: treats a percentage as a fixed amount independent of the whole — '25% off means £25 off' or '20% of 60 is 20'.
Denominator-as-decimal / faulty equivalent: converts 1/5 to 0.5 (copies the 5) or thinks 1/5 = 15%.
Rote 'divide by 100' with no meaning: divides by 100 and stops, or divides by the wrong number (e.g. by 20 for 20%).
Solves '25% off' by finding 25% and forgetting to subtract, giving the discount as the sale price.

activities.title: Live percentage bar over a settable amount
steps: Set the whole amount to £40 on a percentage bar and move a marker to 25%; read off the shaded amount (£10) and a separate sale-price readout (£30), so discount and remaining stay distinct.
Build 20% of 60 by stacking two 10% benchmark blocks (10% of 60 = 6, so 20% = 12), watching the arithmetic appear as you combine them.
Keep the marker at 25% but change the whole from £40 to £80 and observe the pounds answer change from £10 to £20 — the same percentage, a different amount.
Try each target percentage two ways where possible (e.g. 1/5 of 60 as 60 ÷ 5, and 20% of 60 as double 10%) and compare.
activities.insight: A percentage is a proportion of the whole, not a fixed amount: changing the whole changes the pounds answer. Benchmark percentages (50%, 10%, 1%, 25%) can be combined to reach any whole-number target percentage, and the discount is a different quantity from the sale price.

activities.title: Hundred-grid reference for landmark equivalents
steps: Shade 1/5 of a 10×10 hundred-grid and count the squares (20 of 100), then read it simultaneously as 1/5 = 20 hundredths = 0.2 = 20%.
Shade 1/4 to reveal 25 squares = 25% = 0.25, and 3/4 to reveal 75 squares = 75% = 0.75.
Contrast 1/5 (20 squares) with 1/2 (50 squares) to check against the 'copy the denominator digit' habit (1/5 is not 0.5 or 15%).
Derive 2/5 and 4/5 from 1/5 by counting 40 and 80 squares, building the recall set as a connected web rather than separate facts.
activities.insight: 'Per cent means per hundred': the fraction, hundredths-decimal and percentage are three readings of the same shaded quantity on a hundred-grid, and related fractions (2/5, 4/5) derive from 1/5.

activities.title: Fluency and context-step rehearsal
steps: Match the three equivalent forms: 1/5 ↔ 20% ↔ 0.2 and 3/4 ↔ 75% ↔ 0.75.
Complete fill-in-the-blank computations such as '20% of 60 = __' and '1/5 of 60 = __'.
Answer a contextual item: a shop offers 25% off a £40 item — what is the sale price? Watch for the trap of £10 (that is the discount, not the price) and £25 (base-neglect, '25% off = £25').
Explain, for at least one item, a second route to the same answer (e.g. 20% of 60 via 10% of 60 doubled).
activities.insight: Fluent recall of the equivalents must combine with the context subtract-step: finding the discount is not the same as finding the sale price.

checkQuestion: A coat costs £40 and there is 25% off. Work out the sale price and show your method. Then tell me the percentage and the decimal that are equal to 1/5, and use that to find 1/5 of 60.
checkAnswer: 25% of £40 = £10 (a quarter of 40), so the sale price is £40 − £10 = £30. 1/5 = 20% = 0.2, and 1/5 of 60 = 60 ÷ 5 = 12 (equivalently 20% of 60 = 12).
